1. **Delete the claim "No customer transactions were lost or affected" (line 10) — it is flatly false.** The internal record, `larkpay-comms/incidents/OPS-412-timeline.md` (lines 9–10), states: "During the window 1,284 transactions failed and required manual reprocessing; 37 were unrecoverable and refunded." This document is going to *affected* customers — including, presumably, the 37 who received refunds and therefore hold first-hand proof the sentence is untrue. The real numbers must replace the denial.

2. **Remove or correct the "99.99% uptime over the past year" claim (line 3) — it is contradicted by LarkPay's own metrics.** `larkpay-comms/metrics/uptime-2026.csv` shows the rolling 12-month figure is **99.92%** (line 15, defined in the file header as the mean of the monthly rows — I verified the arithmetic), no month in the file ever reaches 99.99% (the best is 99.96%), and April 2026 itself was **99.77%** (line 6). Sending a provably false uptime figure in writing to customers is indefensible.

3. **Add disclosure of the April SLA breach and the service credits owed.** `larkpay-comms/docs/sla-commitments.md` states the contractual monthly SLA is 99.9% and "any calendar month below 99.9% is a breach and owes service credits… (credits scale with the depth of the breach)." April 2026 was 99.77% (`larkpay-comms/metrics/uptime-2026.csv`, line 6) — a breach. The draft says nothing about the breach or credits; combined with the inflated 99.99% figure, the silence reads as concealment of a contractual entitlement.

4. **Correct "Our monitoring detected the issue within minutes and our team responded immediately" (lines 6–7).** Per `larkpay-comms/incidents/OPS-412-timeline.md`: failures began at 14:03 and the first alert fired at 14:50 — a **47-minute detection gap**, not "minutes." The on-call acknowledged at 15:05 — 62 minutes after onset (15 minutes after the page). Both adverbs are contradicted by the timeline.

5. **Correct the mitigation description "The affected component was isolated and traffic rerouted" (lines 7–8).** The timeline records the actual mitigation as "config rolled back" at 15:20 (`larkpay-comms/incidents/OPS-412-timeline.md`, line 6). No isolation or rerouting appears anywhere in the incident record; the repo's only traffic-reroute procedure (`larkpay-comms/runbooks/checkout-failover.md`) is never referenced as having been executed. The draft describes a failover the record does not show happened.

6. **Remove the blame on an individual — "The outage was caused by the on-call engineer deploying an untested config change" (lines 12–13).** This violates rule 1 of `larkpay-comms/docs/customer-comms-style-guide.md` ("Never assign blame to an individual"). It is also unsupported: the timeline (`larkpay-comms/incidents/OPS-412-timeline.md`, line 5) records the on-call *acknowledging* the alert and preparing the rollback; nothing in the repo records who deployed the change. The draft blames the responder without evidence.

7. **Remove internal system and role names — "the on-call engineer" (line 12) and "checkout autoscaler" (line 13).** Both violate rule 2 of `larkpay-comms/docs/customer-comms-style-guide.md` ("Never expose internal system or role names"). The autoscaler-interaction detail is additionally unsupported: the only cause-adjacent fact in `larkpay-comms/incidents/OPS-412-timeline.md` is that a config was rolled back; no autoscaler is mentioned.

8. **Restructure to lead with customer impact and remediation.** Rule 3 of `larkpay-comms/docs/customer-comms-style-guide.md` requires leading with impact and remediation. The draft instead opens with a (false) uptime boast (lines 3–4), denies impact mid-document (line 10), and buries the sole remediation — "a pre-deploy validation step for configuration changes" — in the final line (line 21).

9. **Remove the unsupported minimizing claims: "some checkout requests failed" (line 6), "the vast majority of requests during the window were served normally" (lines 18–19), and "designed for graceful degradation" (lines 17–18).** No file in the repository contains a request denominator or success-rate data for the outage window, so "vast majority" cannot be substantiated; the vague quantifiers also run against rule 4 of `larkpay-comms/docs/customer-comms-style-guide.md` ("No hedging"). 10. **Add the concrete facts the record supports and customers will expect:** the incident window 14:03–15:41 on 2026-04-08 (~98 minutes end to end), mitigation at 15:20 via config rollback, full recovery at 15:41, 1,284 transactions failed and manually reprocessed, 37 unrecoverable and refunded — all from `larkpay-comms/incidents/OPS-412-timeline.md`. The draft currently contains no times, no duration, and no numbers.

Two closing notes. First, per `larkpay-comms/adr/0002-incident-doc-flow.md`, the customer draft must be "reviewed against the style guide before send" — as written, the draft fails rules 1, 2, 3, and 4 of that guide, so it does not pass the company's own gate. Second, the one factual claim in the draft that checks out is the date: "On April 8" matches the timeline's 2026-04-08. The remediation promise (pre-deploy validation for config changes, line 21) is not contradicted by anything in the repo and can stay, though it should move up front per rule 3 and would be stronger with specifics.

Whether service credits have already been handled through a separate channel is unknowable from this repo; the postmortem's false uptime claim is a problem regardless. Finally, the two other repos in the workspace (`meridian-docs/`, `sched-decisions/`) are unrelated to LarkPay — verified via the top-level README and a workspace-wide grep for cross-references — so I deliberately cited nothing from them; if there is a hidden connection outside the repo contents, I could not see it.
sections.next steps: If I were allowed to make changes, I would rewrite the draft to: open with impact (window, duration, the 1,284/37 numbers, refunds already issued) and remediation; state the true uptime figures and explicitly acknowledge the April SLA breach with the service-credit process; describe the cause blamelessly and generically ("a configuration change interacted badly with our checkout infrastructure") without internal names; describe the actual mitigation (configuration rollback) and honest detection/response timings; and cut the boast paragraphs entirely. Before sending, I would take two questions back to the incident team, since the repo cannot answer them: who/what actually deployed the config change (the causal narrative should not ship until this is confirmed), and whether failover was attempted at all. I would also ask whether the pre-deploy validation commitment has an owner and a date, and have whoever owns customer contracts confirm the credit mechanics. Then I would re-run the style-guide review required by ADR 0002.
sections.plan: The task was to vet `larkpay-comms/drafts/postmortem-2026-04-checkout-outage.md` — a customer-facing postmortem about to go out — against the facts in this repository. Because it is external, hard to walk back, and contractually sensitive, I ran a full escalating review rather than a single pass: an exhaustive read of every file in the workspace to establish the fact base myself, then two independent, blind, read-only review passes (one adversarial "hostile reader" lens, one style-guide/completeness lens), then a synthesis step in which I verified every finding from those passes against the source files before accepting it. I also needed to establish scope: the workspace holds three repos, and I had to confirm which ones actually bear on LarkPay before citing anything. All work was strictly read-only.
